Before becoming the ninth Secretary-General of the United Nations in 2017, this Portuguese Socialist led his country as prime minister from 1995 to 2002 — who is he?
António Guterres (born 30 April 1949) is a Portuguese and East Timorese politician and diplomat who, since 2017, has served as the ninth Secretary-General of the United Nations.

Book of Ezekiel is the third of the Latter Prophets in the Tanakh (Hebrew Bible) and one of the major prophetic books in the Christian Bible, where it follows Isaiah and Jeremiah.

Charles G. Dawes (August 27, 1865 - April 23, 1951) was the 30th vice president of the United States from 1925 to 1929 under President Calvin Coolidge.
When a 1952 coup destroyed Cuba's emerging democracy, a young lawyer named Fidel Castro tried first through the courts—then took up arms. Which revolution overthrew Fulgencio Batista's dictatorship?
Cuban Revolution was the military and political movement that overthrew the dictatorship of Fulgencio Batista, who had ruled Cuba from 1952 to 1959.

Harold Shipman (14 January 1946 - 13 January 2004) was an English doctor in general practice and serial killer.
Formed in 1942 from earlier Polish resistance cells, this underground force became one of WWII Europe's largest, fighting German occupiers under London-exiled leadership — which organization?
Home Army (abbreviated AK) was the dominant resistance movement in German-occupied Poland during World War II.
Nicknamed "Bougie," this former Knesset member and welfare minister followed his father into Israel's presidency in 2021 — who is he?
Isaac Herzog (born 22 September 1960) is an Israeli politician who has been serving since 2021 as the president of Israel.
The second son of one president and younger brother of another, this Republican politician served as Florida's governor from 1999 to 2007 before an unsuccessful 2016 presidential bid. Who is he?
Jeb Bush (born February 11, 1953) is an American politician and businessman who served as the 43rd governor of Florida from 1999 to 2007.
After ascending to Judah's throne at age eight, this king ordered major religious reforms once a long-lost scroll of the Law turned up during temple repairs — who is he?
Josiah or Yoshiyahu (Biblical Hebrew) was the 16th king of Judah (c. 640-609 BC).
Backed early on by the Viet Cong and Chinese Communists, this force grew in the forests of eastern Cambodia and later ruled the country as Democratic Kampuchea — which movement was it?
Khmer Rouge is the name that was popularly given to members of the Communist Party of Kampuchea (CPK), and by extension to Democratic Kampuchea, which ruled Cambodia between 1975 and 1979.
He joined the Communist youth league in 1923 and rose to run the Soviet Union for eighteen years, longer than anyone but Stalin — which leader?
Leonid Brezhnev (19 December 1906 - 10 November 1982) was a Soviet politician who served as General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from 1964 until his death in 1982.

Mahua Moitra (Bengali; born 12 October 1974) is an Indian politician and former investment banker.
Dubbed the 'Father of the Steam Navy' for modernizing the fleet, this officer commanded ships in the War of 1812 before ending Japan's isolation — who was he?
Matthew C. Perry (April 10, 1794 - March 4, 1858) was a United States Navy officer who commanded ships in several wars, including the War of 1812 and the Mexican-American War.

After her three-time-president husband died in exile, this Panamanian widow took over both his coffee business and his political party — then in 1999 became the only woman ever to be elected president of Panama. Who is she?

This Pakistani military officer overthrew Nawaz Sharif's government in a 1999 coup and went on to serve as the country's tenth president — who is he?
Pervez Musharraf (11 August 1943 - 5 February 2023) was a Pakistani politician and military officer who served as the tenth president of Pakistan from 2001 to 2008.

This Pennsylvania state treasurer, convicted of accepting a bribe in a state tax-processing scandal, shocked the nation by taking his own life live on camera during a 1987 press conference — who was he?
R. Budd Dwyer (November 21, 1939 - January 22, 1987) was an American politician who served as the 70th treasurer of Pennsylvania from 1981 until his suicide in 1987.
A right-wing populist with a reputation as abrasive and aggressive, this former cost accountant served as New Zealand's prime minister from 1975 to 1984. Who was he?
Robert Muldoon (25 September 1921 - 5 August 1992) was a New Zealand politician who served as the 31st prime minister of New Zealand, from 1975 to 1984, while leader of the National Party.
Said to fly through the night sky on Christmas Eve pulled by reindeer, this legendary gift-giver traces back to a 4th-century Greek bishop known for secret generosity — who is he?

Nyx: Ancient Greek goddess of the night. In ancient Greek art, Nyx often appears alongside other celestial deities such as Selene, Helios and Eos, as a winged figure driving a horse-pulled chariot.

After defeating his half-brother Sviatopolk in a war for the throne, this son of Vladimir the Great ruled Kiev from 1019 to 1054 — who was he?
Yaroslav the Wise: Grand Prince of Kiev from 1019 to 1054.
This French lawyer-turned-politician served as prime minister under Emmanuel Macron from 2017 to 2020, then returned to serve as mayor of Le Havre — who is he?
Édouard Philippe: Prime Minister of France from 2017 to 2020. A lawyer by occupation, Philippe is a former member of the Union for a Popular Movement (UMP), which later became The Republicans (LR).
Which of these four is the eldest?
Eratosthenes (born 276 BC) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below was born first?
Henry Vaughan (born 1621) is the earliest of the four. Henry Vaughan (1621 – 23 April 1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet, author and translator writing in English, and a medical physician.
Which of these people was born first?
Ryōkichi Yatabe (born 1851) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below is best known as an astronomer?
Toghon Temür is an astronomer. Toghon Temür acceded to the throne in 1333 after years of succession disputes following his father's death.
Which one below is best known as a mathematician?
Omar Khayyam is a mathematician. Omar Khayyam (1048–1131) was a Persian poet and polymath, known for his contributions to mathematics, astronomy, philosophy, and Persian literature.
What is the atomic number of Barium?
Barium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ba and atomic number 56.
What is the atomic number of Nickel?
Nickel is a chemical element; it has symbol Ni and atomic number 28.
In what year did J. Robert Oppenheimer die?
J. Robert Oppenheimer: In 1941, Oppenheimer was briefed about nuclear weapon design by Australian physicist Mark Oliphant.
In what year was Mass–energy equivalence discovered?
Mass–energy equivalence: In physics, mass–energy equivalence is the relationship between mass and energy in a system's rest frame.
Which company manufactures Harrier jump jet?
Harrier jump jet: Hawker Siddeley. The Harrier emerged as the only truly successful V/STOL design of the many attempted during that era.
NHIndustries NH90: Airbus Helicopters. The NHIndustries NH90 is a medium-sized European twin-engine multi-role military helicopter.
Who is credited with discovering Zirconium?
Zirconium: Martin Heinrich Klaproth. Zirconium is a chemical element; it has symbol Zr and atomic number 40.
Who is credited with discovering Quetzalcoatlus?
Quetzalcoatlus: Douglas A. Lawson. Quetzalcoatlus is a genus of azhdarchid pterosaur that lived during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous in North America.
Who is credited with discovering Silicon carbide?
Silicon carbide: Edward Goodrich Acheson. Silicon carbide (SiC), also known as carborundum, is a hard chemical compound of silicon and carbon.
Who is credited with discovering Bromine?
Bromine: Carl Jacob Löwig. Bromine is a chemical element; it has symbol Br and atomic number 35.

A German-born theoretical physicist best known for developing the theory of relativity, his mass–energy formula E=mc2 comes from special relativity and has been called "the world's most famous equation." Born in 1879, who won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics?
Albert Einstein (14 March 1879 - 18 April 1955) was a German-born theoretical physicist best known for developing the known theory of relativity.

Affecting roughly 1 in 15,000 people, this rare genetic disorder impairs the nervous system, causing severe intellectual disability and little to no speech, but is also linked to an unusually happy demeanor — what's it called?
Angelman syndrome (AS) is a rare genetic disorder that affects approximately 1 in 15,000 individuals.

This type of blood vessel typically carries oxygen-rich blood away from the heart, though the vessels serving the lungs and an unborn baby's placenta carry deoxygenated blood instead — what's it called?
Artery (from Greek (artr)) is a blood vessel in humans and most other animals that takes oxygenated blood away from the heart in the systemic circulation to one or more parts of the body.
Found in almost every habitat except the open sea and the poles, the order Coleoptera is the largest of all and accounts for about a quarter of every known animal species — which insects are these?
Beetle are insects that form the order Coleoptera, in the superorder Holometabola.
The third-most-produced bomber in history, this American four-engine heavy bomber dominated the European Theater and dropped more bombs than any other plane in WWII — which aircraft is it?
Boeing B-17 Flying Fortress is an American four-engined heavy bomber aircraft that was developed in the mid-1930s for the United States Army Air Corps (USAAC).
This Indian physicist discovered, with his student, that light changes wavelength when passing through a transparent material — a phenomenon now named for him — earning a 1930 Nobel Prize. Who is he?
C. V. Raman (7 November 1888 - 21 November 1970) was an Indian physicist known for his work in the field of light scattering.
Belonging to the trumpet-vine family Bignoniaceae, this tree genus thrives across warm parts of North America, the Caribbean, and East Asia — what is it called?
Catalpa is a genus of flowering plants in the family Bignoniaceae, native to warm temperate and subtropical regions of North America, the Caribbean, and East Asia.
Native to East Asia and blooming late in the season, these autumn flowers of the daisy family are associated in the Northern Hemisphere with the month of November. What flower is it?
Chrysanthemum (kriss-), sometimes abbreviated to mums or chrysanths, are perennial herbaceous flowering plants in the family Asteraceae that bloom in the autumn.
Known by a colorful nickname, this inflammation of the clear layer over the white of the eye turns it pink, may leave it stuck shut by morning, and spreads easily — what is it?
Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva, the thin and clear layer that covers the white surface of the eye and the inner eyelid.

Known for names like thornapple, jimsonweed, and devil's trumpet, this genus of nine extremely poisonous, night-blooming plants in the nightshade family can cause hallucinations and delirium if ingested — what is it?
Datura is a genus of nine species of highly poisonous, vespertine-flowering plants belonging to the nightshade family (Solanaceae).

Its name comes from a Greek word meaning 'deed' or 'act,' and Aristotle's Poetics contrasted it with the epic and lyric modes; two masks for comedy and tragedy are its emblem. What mode of fiction is it?
Drama is the specific mode of fiction represented in performance: a play, opera, mime, ballet, etc., performed in a theatre, or on radio or television.
Noted for producing one of the most variable litter sizes of any dog breed, this active gun dog comes in 'field' and 'house' varieties and gave rise to its American cousin breed — what is it?
English Cocker Spaniel is a breed of gun dog. It is noteworthy for producing one of the most varied numbers of pups in a litter among all dog breeds.
Immature at birth but developed by puberty, this network of organs includes the vagina, uterus, and fallopian tubes, protected by a fold called the labia majora — what's it called?
Female reproductive system is made up of the internal and external sex organs that function in the reproduction of new offspring.
This Canadian physician and author has written five books exploring how childhood trauma shapes conditions from ADHD to addiction, arguing recovery must address underlying emotional pain — who is he?
Gabor Maté (born January 1944) is a Canadian physician and author.
This term describes the overall system of processes, rules, and power structures that sets boundaries of conduct and steers the direction of an organized group — what is it?

Governance is the overall complex system or framework of processes, functions, structures, rules, laws and norms born out of the relationships, interactions, power dynamics and communication within an organized group of individuals.

His synergy with information-theory father Claude Shannon laid foundations for the Information Age, and during WWII he helped build automatic guns that defended London from V-1 flying bombs — who was this Dutch-American control-theory pioneer?
Hendrik Wade Bode (-d,; December 24, 1905 - June 21, 1982) was an American engineer, researcher, inventor, author and scientist, of Dutch ancestry.
Often caused by kidney failure or certain blood-pressure medications, this condition means too much potassium in the blood, with levels above 5.5 mmol/L — what's it called?
Hyperkalemia is an elevated level of potassium (K+) in the blood.
With the formula Fe2O3, this reddish inorganic compound occurs naturally as the mineral hematite, a key raw material for the steel industry — which compound?
Iron(III) oxide is the inorganic compound with the formula Fe2O3. It occurs in nature as the mineral hematite, which serves as the primary source of iron for the steel industry.
Famed first for studying diamagnetism, which Irish physicist proved in 1859 the link between atmospheric CO2 and what we now call the greenhouse effect?
John Tyndall (2 August 1820 - 4 December 1893) was an Irish physicist.

Born of Peranakan Chinese cuisine and beloved in Singapore and Malaysia, this spicy noodle dish swims in a rich coconut-curry soup soured with tamarind, topped with prawns or chicken — what's its name?
Laksa is a spicy noodle dish popular in Southeast Asia.
Named from the Greek word for 'stone,' this alkali metal with symbol Li tarnishes from silver to black in air and was once mined mainly from pegmatite minerals — what is it?
Lithium (from Ancient) is a chemical element; it has symbol Li and atomic number 3.

Native to the temperate Northern Hemisphere, this genus of 32 to 57 deciduous trees and shrubs in the rose family includes the ancestors of a familiar orchard fruit plus ornamental wild and crab varieties — what's the genus?
Malus (or) is a genus of about 32-57 species of small deciduous trees or shrubs in the family Rosaceae, including the domesticated orchard apple, crab apples, and wild apples.
Together with the Focke-Wulf Fw 190, this monoplane fighter formed the backbone of the Luftwaffe's fighter force throughout the Second World War. What aircraft is it?
Messerschmitt Bf 109 is a monoplane fighter aircraft that was designed and initially produced by the German aircraft manufacturer Bayerische Flugzeugwerke (BFW).
Also called Indian mulberry, this tropical fruit tree contains harmful anthraquinones, and its foul-smelling fruit is mostly eaten only as a famine food — which species is it?
Morinda citrifolia is a fruit-bearing tree in the coffee family, Rubiaceae.
This multidisciplinary field studies the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves — their function and their disorders — blending physiology, anatomy, and more — name the field?
Neuroscience is the scientific study of the nervous system (the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nervous system), its functions, and its disorders.
Its name means 'serpent-bearer' in Ancient Greek — this large constellation straddling the celestial equator is depicted as a man grasping a snake — name it?
Ophiuchus (o-fee-) is a large constellation straddling the celestial equator.
This English amateur astronomer joined an astronomy association at age 11, compiled the Caldwell catalogue, and hosted the BBC's record-breaking 'The Sky at Night' — who was he?
Patrick Moore (4 March 1923 - 9 December 2012) was an English amateur astronomer who attained prominence in that field as a writer, researcher, radio commentator and television presenter.

This branch of linguistics studies how languages organize their foundational sound units — like the contrast between 'bat' and 'gnat' — or, in sign languages, elements like hand shape and location — what is it called?
Phonology (formerly also phonemics or phonematics) is the branch of linguistics that concerns how languages organize the foundational elements that make their words.
Native to cool temperate regions of the Old World, which poplar species is commonly known as European or quaking aspen?
Populus tremula (commonly called aspen, common aspen, Eurasian aspen, European aspen, or quaking aspen) is a species of poplar native to cool temperate regions of the Old World.
This kidney inflammation, most often caused by E. coli infection, typically causes fever and tenderness along the side of the body — what is it?
Pyelonephritis is inflammation of the kidney, typically due to a bacterial infection.
Made up of a large and small subunit built from RNA and proteins, this molecular machine found in every living cell translates messenger RNA into chains of amino acids — what is it?
Ribosome is a ribonucleoprotein particle found in all cells, both prokaryotic and eukaryotic, responsible for the synthesis of proteins.
Nicknamed the seven-year itch, this contagious skin condition is caused by a microscopic burrowing mite and thrives in crowded places like prisons and care homes — what is it?
Scabies (also sometimes known as the seven-year itch) is a contagious human skin infestation by the tiny (0.2-0.45 mm) mite Sarcoptes scabiei, variety hominis.
With the formula AgNO3, this colorless, highly water-soluble compound is the least expensive salt of a lustrous precious metal and a precursor to many similar compounds — name it?
Silver nitrate is an inorganic compound with chemical formula AgNO3.
Defined as exactly 101,325 pascals and roughly equal to Earth's average sea-level air pressure, what is this reference unit of pressure called?
Standard atmosphere (unit) (symbol: atm) is a unit of pressure defined as 101325 Pa.
Appointed a government economic minister in 1991, this academic rose to become prime minister of Turkey in 1993 and later served as its foreign minister — who is she?
Tansu Çiller (born 24 May 1946) is a Turkish academic, economist, and politician who served as the 22nd prime minister of Turkey from 1993 to 1996.

Proposing an information management system in March 1989 and implementing the first successful client-server exchange that November, this English computer scientist invented HTML, HTTP and the URL system — who is he?
Tim Berners-Lee (born 8 June 1955), also known as TimBL, is an English computer scientist best known as the inventor of the World Wide Web, HTML, the URL system, and HTTP.
Lined with a type of tissue called transitional epithelium, this narrow tube can develop kidney stones or reflux problems and connects each kidney to the bladder — what is it?
Ureter are tubes composed of smooth muscle that transport urine from the kidneys to the urinary bladder.

First cultivated in the Fertile Crescent around 9600 BC, this cereal grass genus is grown on more land worldwide than any other food crop, with varieties including spelt, durum, and einkorn — name the crop?
Wheat is a group of wild and domesticated grasses of the genus Triticum.
The only living member of its entire mammalian order, this nocturnal African burrower uses its long snout and powerful claws to dig ants and termites out of their mounds — what animal is it?
Aardvark: Burrowing mammal native to Africa.
While bacteria and some plants may be biologically immortal, this universal process in humans slows reaction time even as knowledge tends to grow — what is it called?
Ageing: Biological process of getting older.
This genus of over 650 succulent species includes a 'true' member long used in pharmaceutical products, native to Africa, Madagascar, and the Arabian Peninsula — which genus?
Aloe: Genus of succulent flowering plants.
Struck off the medical register for 'serious professional misconduct,' this former surgeon authored the fraudulent 1998 Lancet paper falsely tying the MMR vaccine to autism — who is he?
This inflammatory condition causes right lower abdominal pain and is commonly triggered by a blockage from a calcified mass of feces called a fecalith — what is it?
Known medically as tinea pedis, this common fungal infection often begins between the toes and spreads in places like swimming pools and locker rooms — what is it?
Athlete's foot: Skin infection caused by fungus.
Bred in Britain to hunt rabbits and hares, this scent hound's keen nose also makes it a popular detection dog for smuggled food at airports — which breed?
Beagle: Breed of small scent hound. The Beagle is a British breed of scent hound, similar in appearance to the much larger foxhound.
Patented in 1976 and sold under the brand name Zebeta, this beta-1-selective medication treats high blood pressure and heart failure — what is it?
Bisoprolol: Beta-1 selective adrenenergic blocker medication used to treat cardiovascular diseases.

Unlike most elements, this one is forged entirely by cosmic-ray spallation and supernovae rather than stellar fusion, and is mined from evaporite minerals like borax, mostly in Turkey — which element?
Boron: Chemical element with atomic number 5 (B)
Unlike benzodiazepines, this anti-anxiety medication doesn't cause sedation or dependence, and works through serotonin 5-HT1A receptors with a delayed onset of two to four weeks — which drug?
Buspirone: Medication used to treat anxiety disorders.
Domesticated in Mexico roughly 6,000 years ago, this nightshade produces berries used in cooking, medicine, and even self-defense sprays — which plant species is it?
Capsicum annuum: Species of flowering plant in the nightshade family.
Originally called 'centigrade' from Latin words for a hundred and steps, this SI temperature scale was renamed in 1948 to honor the Swedish astronomer who proposed it in 1742 — which scale?
Celsius: Unit of measurement for temperature.

The second-lightest halogen, this yellow-green gas is so reactive it has the highest electron affinity of any element and once fascinated medieval alchemists heating chloride salts — which element is it?
Chlorine: Chemical element with atomic number 17 (Cl)
Native to the Americas from Mexico to South America, this diurnal member of the Procyonidae family goes by the name 'quash' in Belize — what is it?

Known to NATO by the reporting name 'Mop' and to Canadian forces as the Canso, this WWII flying boat served every branch of the U.S. military and remained in some air forces into the 1980s — which aircraft?
Consolidated PBY Catalina: American 1930s flying boat.
Native to the Irano-Turanian region, this flowering plant's dried seeds season cuisines worldwide, despite no strong evidence backing its use in traditional medicine — which spice?
Cumin: Species of plant with seeds used as a spice.
Often tied to diseases like Alzheimer's, this incurable, progressive syndrome erodes memory, language, and motivation in stages — which condition is being described?
Spanning some 40 species from oceanic to river-dwelling and ranging down to a human-sized 1.7 meters, these toothed whales are kin to belugas and porpoises — what are they?
Dolphin: Informal classification of marine mammals, closely related to whales and porpoises.
This American astronomer proved that many so-called nebulae were actually separate galaxies, and in 1929 showed that galaxies recede faster the farther away they are — who is he?
Triggered by the parasympathetic nervous system and a rise in nitric oxide, this physiological event leaves an organ firm and engorged — what is it?
Erection: Physiological phenomenon involving the hardening and enlargement of the penis.

Also known as the wisent, this species is the heaviest wild land mammal on its continent — hunted to extinction in the wild by the early 20th century before being restored through captive breeding programs. Which animal?
European bison: Eurasian species of mammal. It is one of two extant species of bison, alongside the American bison.
This genus of about 850 tropical tree, shrub, and vine species is best known for two cultivated fruit-bearing members and serves as a vital food source for wildlife across the tropics — which genus?
Ficus: Genus of flowering plants in the mulberry family Moraceae.
Before becoming Ferrari's Formula One team principal in 2023, this Frenchman co-founded a junior-racing outfit that won back-to-back titles with Lewis Hamilton and Nico Rosberg — who is he?
Combining Greek words for 'earth,' 'form,' and 'study,' what field examines how landscapes and seafloor features form and evolve over time?
This common name covers edible fruit from the Ribes genus — the same genus as currants — coming in colors from green and red to purple, yellow, white, or black — which fruit?
Gooseberry: Species of Ribes cultivated for its edible fruit.
Producing up to a hundred billion new cells a day from specialized stem cells, this biological process manufactures every component of blood — what is it?
Haematopoiesis: Formation of blood cellular components.
Introduced to Britain in the 19th century as an ornamental plant, this Caucasus-native's sap causes painful blistering burns when exposed skin meets sunlight — which species?
Heracleum mantegazzianum: Species of flowering plant. Heracleum mantegazzianum, commonly known as giant hogweed, is a monocarpic perennial herbaceous plant in the carrot family Apiaceae.

In the Renaissance this field of study covered classical literature and language rather than religion or divinity, and today it groups subjects using critical and interpretive methods rather than empirical ones — what broad academic category is this?
Humanities: Academic disciplines that study society and culture.

Trained originally as a naval architect before becoming a self-taught nuclear physicist, this scientist directed the Soviet Union's atomic bomb program and earned the nickname 'father of the Russian bomb' — who is he?
This tech entrepreneur co-founded Twitter, later built a fintech company behind Square, Cash App, and Tidal, and also helped launch the decentralized network Bluesky?
As a Princeton grad student this mathematician dreamed up an "equilibrium" concept that won him a 1994 Nobel in Economics — who was he?
John Forbes Nash Jr.: American mathematician and Nobel Laureate (1928–2015)
Born in Kabul to a diplomat, this Afghan-American physician-turned-novelist wrote the bestselling 'The Kite Runner' before serving as a UNHCR goodwill ambassador — who is he?
Khaled Hosseini: Afghan-American novelist (born 1965). Hosseini's novels have spread awareness about Afghanistan's people and culture.
He fathered the Ford Mustang in the 1960s, then rescued Chrysler from collapse as its CEO in the 1980s — one of the rare executives to run two of Detroit's Big Three. Who?
A Chinese computer engineer turned science-fiction author, he won the Hugo Award for The Three-Body Problem and the Locus Award for its sequel, Death's End. Who is he?
Liu Cixin: Chinese science fiction writer (born 1963)
First synthesized in 1912 by a Merck chemist, this stimulant known on the street as ecstasy or molly became linked to raves and electronic dance music in the 1980s — which drug?
MDMA: Psychoactive drug, often called ecstasy.
Whether a milk board's 'Got Milk?' campaign or a city pitching itself as a tourist destination, this discipline boils down to acquiring, satisfying, and retaining customers — what is it?
Marketing: Study and process of exploring, creating, and delivering value to customers.
More than 80% of cases of this cancer — which grows in the thin lining covering the lungs and other organs — trace back to asbestos exposure. What is it?
Named for the Latin for 'thousand feet,' no species of this many-legged arthropod class was confirmed to have 1,000-plus legs until a 2020 discovery with over 1,300 — what are they?
Millipede: Class of arthropods. Its primary defence mechanism is to curl into a tight coil, thereby protecting its legs and other vital delicate areas on the body behind a hard exoskeleton.
Grown above the upper lip and below the nose, this facial hair style has taken many forms across history — what is it called?
Moustache: Strip of facial hair across the upper lip. A moustache (UK:) or mustache (US:) is a growth of facial hair grown above the upper lip and under the nose of men.

Attributed to 19th-century pathologist Rudolf Virchow, this term for the premature death of cells caused by trauma or infection contrasts with the body's own programmed cell death — what's the condition called?
Necrosis: Unprogrammed cell death caused by external cell injury.
This carnivorous freshwater fish, found widely across cold waters worldwide, has a current all-tackle world record of 25 kg, caught in Germany in 1986 — what species is it?
Northern pike: Species of fish. The northern pike (Esox lucius), also known as jack, northern or simply pike, is a species of carnivorous fish of the genus Esox (pikes).

Sitting between tissue and a full body system in life's hierarchy, this general term describes a structural unit built from functional tissue (parenchyma) plus supportive tissue (stroma), as seen in the intestinal wall — what is such a unit called?
Organ (biology): Collection of tissues with similar functions.
Often triggered by nail-biting or frequent hand-washing, this inflammation of the skin around the nail is usually bacterial when sudden and fungal when it drags on — what is it called?
Paronychia: Inflammation of skin surrounding a nail. Its sudden (acute) occurrence is usually due to the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus.
Featuring an R−O−O−R backbone where two oxygen atoms bond directly to each other, what name covers this class of molecules?
Peroxide: Chemical compounds with the structure R–O–O–R'

The most economically important member of the bromeliad family, this South American fruit became a 17th-century European symbol of luxury — and forms when many small flowers fuse into one — what is it?
Pineapple: Species of flowering plant in the family Bromeliaceae.
This deliquescent white salt helps make Dutch-process cocoa, soap, and glass, and can also turn up leaking from old alkaline batteries — what compound?
Potassium carbonate: Chemical compound. It is a white salt, which is soluble in water and forms a strongly alkaline solution.

Marked by delusions, hallucinations and disorganized thinking, this state — not a diagnosis itself — often stems from schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or alcohol-related brain damage — what is it called?
Psychosis: Abnormal condition of the mind.
Also called broccoli rabe, this bitter, vitamin K-rich cruciferous vegetable is a Mediterranean cuisine staple with edible leaves, buds, and stems — what is it?
This blue supergiant in Orion, also known as Beta Orionis, outshines the Sun by up to 363,000 times and anchors a system of at least four stars — which star?
Rigel: Brightest star in the constellation Orion.
Named after the Latin word for willow tree, from which it was first derived, this plant hormone and aspirin precursor shows up in anti-acne cosmetics — what is it?
Salicylic acid: Chemical compound used in medicines and industry.
These marine algae include the kelps that shelter fisheries and are estimated to produce at least half of Earth's oxygen — what are they collectively called?
Seaweed: Macroscopic marine algae. Seaweed, or macroalgae, refers to thousands of species of macroscopic, multicellular, marine algae.
This order of fully aquatic, herbivorous mammals includes dugongs and manatees and is more closely related to elephants than to whales — what is it called?
Sirenia: Order of aquatic herbivorous mammals. The Protosirenidae (Eocene sirenians) and Prorastomidae (terrestrial sirenians) families are extinct.
With eight legs, venom-injecting fangs, and silk-spinning spinnerets, this arthropod has spread to every continent but Antarctica — over 53,000 species and counting. What is it?
Signified by the minus sign, this arithmetic operation represents removing objects from a collection and is the inverse of addition — which operation is it?
Subtraction: One of the four basic arithmetic operations.
This genus of flowering plants, commonly called dandelions, thrives nearly worldwide in yards, gardens, and roadsides — which genus?
Taraxacum: Genus of flowering plants in the family Asteraceae.
Working in his famous "Fly Room" with fruit flies, this American won a Nobel for showing that genes ride on chromosomes — who was he?
Commonly nicknamed a "mini-stroke," this brief disruption of blood flow to the brain causes stroke-like symptoms that fully resolve within 24 hours — what medical event is it?
Transient ischemic attack: Minor form of stroke.
This group of large hoofed mammals splits into odd-toed members like horses and rhinos, and even-toed members like cattle, giraffes, and camels — what are they called?
Ungulate: Group of mammals that walk on the tips of their toes or hooves.
Running a boutique called Sex with partner Malcolm McLaren, this English designer helped bring punk fashion into the mainstream and shaped the look of the Sex Pistols — who is she?
A short-legged, stubby-tailed marsupial native to Australia, this burrowing animal can weigh up to 35 kilograms and survives in an isolated pocket of central Queensland — which creature?
Wombat: Species of marsupial native to Australia.
Protactinium is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for protactinium is Pa. Protactinium is a chemical element; it has symbol Pa and atomic number 91.
